articles.title: Burnham pressed on economy at first PMQs as UK borrowing costs rise
articles.summary: Burnham said he had already cut taxes, including VAT on energy bills and hospitality business rates.
articles.body:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has pressed Andy Burnham over UK borrowing and spending at his first Prime Minister's Questions.

Badenoch called on the PM to say where spending would be cut and how he would deal with the UK's increasing debt, after the cost of borrowing for the UK rose, reaching a new 18-year high on Wednesday.

The PM blamed the previous Conservative government saying that the "turbulence on global markets are because of that exposure that they left behind".

Burnham became prime minister in July, having taken over from Sir Keir Starmer just before Parliament's summer recess, and it was the first time he had faced the Tory leader at the Commons session.

The prime minister used the summer recess to tour the UK, and had announced a series of eye-catching policies, mainly aimed at tackling the cost of living.

MPs returned to Parliament on Tuesday and Burnham spent more than three hours in the Commons, making a statement and answering questions from MPs.

At PMQs, Badenoch said the prime minister had set out plenty of spending plans but no detail of how he would be paying the bill.

"The markets are clearly worried that we now have a spendthrift prime minister who wants to say yes to everyone but cannot tell us where the money is coming from," she said.

"He needs to pay for all his new promises and he has a choice - higher taxes, more borrowing, or spending cuts.

"Yesterday he said change begins with honesty, so will he be honest and tell us: is he preparing to raise taxes again, yes or no?"

Burnham had earlier said he had already cut taxes, including VAT on energy bills and a cut in business rates for hospitality.

"I've already indicated my first moves were to cut tax, but I'm not going to do what any prime minister has done and write the budget here," he said, adding he and Chancellor John Healey had agreed on an early date for the Budget in October to reduce speculation.

At PMQs, Badenoch also raised comments from economist and cross-bench peer Lord Jim O'Neill, who had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser, but who ruled out joining Burnham's government .

Speaking to the BBC, Lord O'Neill had praised the PM for "a great first five weeks" which he said had helped lift consumer and business confidence; adding the current spike in market interest rates for government debt would force Labour to start "dealing with the triple lock" on the state pension, and "excessive" welfare spending.

Badenoch pointed to a warning from Lord O'Neill that the prime minister's tone during his Tuesday Commons debut would have unsettled investors, although the peer had also said that spike was mostly mirroring US market upheaval concerning the Iran conflict.

The PM also sought to stress his administration's fiscal responsibility and said ministers were taking steps to reduce debt.

He said: "This will be a government grounded in fiscal responsibility. It will stick to the fiscal rules, but at the same time, we will help reduce cost-of-living pressure on our constituents, and that's the approach that we will take."

Interest rates on government bonds have been going up, with the yield on a 10-year bond at its highest level since 2008, while the yield on a 30-year bond is at its highest since 1998, meaning it costs the government more to borrow over the long term.

It could mean that the government's choices on what it wants to spend are constrained as the Budget approaches.

"Lord O'Neill, a close friend of the prime minister, said yesterday's statement in the Commons was the last thing investors wanted to hear," Badenoch said.

"Lord O'Neill is a serious economist. He knows what he's talking about and, sure enough, yesterday the cost of government borrowing rose to its highest in 18 years.

"How does he plan to tackle the government's rising debt costs?"

Burnham replied that he and Lord O'Neill did "not always agree", before attacking Badenoch's shadow cabinet reshuffle for bringing MPs who were in the leadership team of former Conservative prime minister Liz Truss back to her front benches.

To shouts of "point-scoring!" from the Conservative side, he said: "Can I also say to her and the whole of her new shadow cabinet, the majority of whom were part of a government that lasted for 49 days, a short-lived government that crashed confidence in the economy and hammered people's mortgages.

"She took a decision at the weekend, she removed a shadow chancellor who said that the Truss mini budget was a mistake, and she replaced that shadow chancellor with one that helped to write the Truss mini budget."

Badenoch said Burnham had not ruled out tax rises, claiming: "The reason why that budget failed was because spending was announced before the money to pay for it, which is exactly what he is doing right now."

Burnham's PMQs debut shows the challenge of delivering new style of politics

Why are UK borrowing costs rising and what does it mean for me?

Burnham promises more devolution and public control of essential services

The opposition leader went on to raise the Russian attack on Leipzig airport in Germany , urging the prime minister to commit to 3% spending.

So far the new government has only committed to meeting the 3.5% spending target for defence by 2035, pushing back the interim 3% spending commitment to spring next year.

The new chancellor quit as defence secretary in June over the last government's failure to commit to a 3% increase, which proved to be the final nail in the coffin for Sir Keir's premiership.

Burnham told MPs: "The very reason I appointed this Chancellor to his position is because of his strong commitment to the defence of our country and to defence spending.

"We will fully fund the defence investment plan and at the spending review we will set out a plan to meet the Nato commitments by 2035, there is no problem with our commitment to defence."

articles.title: Who is Sukhvinder ‘Suki’ Singh Sunger? Turbaned Sikh cop makes history at Edinburgh Military Tattoo
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Canadian police constable Sukhvinder “Suki” Singh Sunger has made history at the 2026 Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo by becoming the first turbaned S.
articles.body: Canadian police constable Sukhvinder “Suki” Singh Sunger has made history at the 2026 Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo by becoming the first turbaned Sikh Drum Major to lead a performance at the iconic event in Scotland.Sunger, a member of the Vancouver Police Department (VPD), led the Vancouver Police Pipe Band onto the Edinburgh Castle Esplanade during the annual spectacle, which brings together military bands, musicians and cultural performers from across the world.Who is Sukhvinder ‘Suki’ Singh Sunger?Sunger is a police constable with the Vancouver Police Department in British Columbia, Canada. Raised in Victoria, he began his policing career as a reserve constable with the Victoria Police Department before joining the VPD in 2002.He has served with the Vancouver Police Department for more than two decades, primarily as a traffic enforcement officer. He holds a diploma in criminal justice and has also served as a United Nations peacekeeper in South Sudan.Beyond policing, Sunger is a prominent member of the Vancouver Police Pipe Band, where he serves as Drum Major.Sikh identity meets Scottish traditionSunger appeared in the band’s traditional Highland dress, wearing a Royal Stewart tartan kilt along with a specially designed ceremonial dastaar instead of the conventional feather bonnet.His appearance brought together two distinct cultural traditions — Sikh identity and Scottish pipe-band heritage — on one of the world's most recognised ceremonial stages.The 2026 Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo, themed “A Call to Gather”, ran from August 7 to 29. Sunger made his debut at the event while leading the Vancouver Police Pipe Band in its fourth appearance.From tenor drum to Drum MajorSunger joined the Vancouver Police Pipe Band around 2018-19, becoming its first Sikh member and first person of colour. He initially played the tenor drum before adding the Punjabi dhol to his performances.In December 2025, he was elected Drum Major for a three-year term, placing him at the front of the band as its leader during major performances and ceremonies.Sunger’s special connection with PunjabSunger travelled to India with the Vancouver Police Pipe Band in 2019 during its tour marking the centenary of the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.The band performed at the Golden Temple in Amritsar, Guru Nanak Dev University and other venues in Punjab. During the tour, Sunger performed on both the Scottish tenor drum and Punjabi dhol, including an arrangement of “Sare Jahan Se Accha”.A milestone for Sikh representationFounded in 1914, the Vancouver Police Pipe Band is the oldest continuously serving non-military pipe band in British Columbia.Sunger's appearance at Edinburgh Castle has drawn attention to Sikh representation in public service and international cultural events. His turban and beard alongside traditional Highland dress offered a striking representation of two distinct cultural traditions coming together on a global stage.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: From 1886 to 1968, more than 20 million fish were stocked in waters that became Rocky Mountain National Park; in 2026 crews treated 14.3 miles to remove non-native fish and restore threatened greenback trout
articles.summary: US News: For more than 80 years, fish were deliberately introduced into the waters that would become Rocky Mountain National Park. According to the National Pa.
articles.body: For more than 80 years, fish were deliberately introduced into the waters that would become Rocky Mountain National Park. According to the National Park Service (NPS), more than 20 million fish were stocked in waters that are now part of Rocky Mountain National Park between 1886 and 1968, most of them non-native trout. What was once intended to support recreational fishing eventually created challenges for native fish and aquatic ecosystems. In 2026, park managers are working to reverse some of those effects. As part of the Poudre Headwaters Project, crews treated waterways connected to the 14.3-mile Grand Ditch to remove non-native fish and prepare habitat for the recovery of the federally threatened greenback cutthroat trout.A long history of stockingFish stocking began in the area in 1886, before Rocky Mountain National Park was established. Colorado stocked fish into mountain waters to create and expand opportunities for recreational fishing. The programme grew over the following decades. Hatcheries were established in Estes Park and Grand Lake, producing large numbers of fish for release into local waters. Some of the introduced species were not naturally found in the region. Fish were even stocked in certain waters that had historically been fishless. By 1968, more than 20 million fish had been introduced into waters that are now part of the national park. Non-native fish had become established across much of the park's aquatic environment.Why the approach changedThe park's fish-management philosophy eventually shifted from increasing fishing opportunities to protecting native ecosystems. The National Park Service issued formal guidance on fish management in 1936, encouraging the use of native fish and discouraging the introduction of non-native species. Stocking in historically fishless waters was also prohibited. By 1968, fish stocking had stopped.However, ending stocking did not remove the non-native trout that were already established. Species such as brook trout remained in streams and could compete with native fish for food and habitat. That left park managers with a more complicated task: removing introduced fish from selected waterways so native species could recover.Restoring greenback troutThe greenback cutthroat trout is one of the native species targeted by the restoration programme. These trout historically occupied Colorado's mountain waters, but their populations have been affected by competition and interactions with introduced fish. Brook trout can compete with greenback cutthroat trout for resources, making the removal of non-native fish an important part of restoring native populations. The aim is not simply to reduce the number of fish in a stream. Instead, managers want to restore waterways where native trout can survive, reproduce and eventually expand their populations.The 2026 projectThe latest work is part of the Poudre Headwaters Project, a large-scale effort to restore native trout habitat in the headwaters of the Cache la Poudre and Colorado River watersheds. The project includes the Grand Ditch, a historic water-diversion system that extends for about 14.3 miles. In August 2026, another phase of the project took place in the Kawuneeche Valley. Some areas were temporarily closed from August 24 to August 30 while crews conducted the work. The treatment targeted non-native fish in the Grand Ditch and connected waterways inside Rocky Mountain National Park.Removing non-native fishCompletely removing fish from remote mountain streams can be difficult using conventional methods. Electrofishing, nets and angling can remove fish in some situations, but they may not be sufficient when managers need to eliminate non-native populations from an entire connected drainage. For the Poudre Headwaters Project, crews use rotenone, a fish toxicant, in targeted waterways. The treatment is controlled to prevent the chemical from affecting areas outside the project zone. Potassium permanganate is used downstream to neutralise rotenone, while the chemical also breaks down naturally over time. This allows crews to treat waterways that would otherwise be difficult to clear completely.A different futureThe work represents a major reversal of a practice that lasted more than eight decades. Fish were once introduced to make mountain waters more attractive to anglers. Today, managers are deliberately removing some of those same introduced species to give native trout a better chance of returning. The restoration will not undo the history of stocking overnight. But by removing non-native fish and restoring suitable habitat, the Poudre Headwaters Project is working toward a landscape where greenback cutthroat trout can once again occupy parts of their native range. The effort shows how conservation priorities can change over time: what was once considered beneficial for recreation can later require active restoration to protect the ecosystem.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Burnham's PMQs debut shows the challenge of delivering new style of politics
articles.summary: Burnham's exchanges with Kemi Badenoch slipped into familiar territory of trading barbs, writes Alex Forsyth.
articles.body:
Throughout the summer Andy Burnham's been attempting to cultivate a new style of communicating with a steady stream of social media videos designed to speak directly to the public.

But alongside his digital push, the prime minister still has to master one of Westminster's weekly traditions; the political back and forth that is Prime Minister's Questions.

To some it might seem outdated in a modern media world, but the exchange across the despatch box is still deemed vital by many in Westminster as a moment of scrutiny; a chance for the public to peer into Parliament's workings and a crucial factor in setting the mood among backbench MPs as they watch – and judge – the performance of party leaders.

So the debut of a new prime minister matters.

Badenoch presses Burnham on borrowing costs at his first Prime Minister's Questions

Burnham took his place in the House of Commons chamber to raucous cheers from the packed Labour benches and struck a confident tone from the start, clearly keen to maintain the sense of optimism he's promised the country.

His initial exchanges with Kemi Badenoch were vaguely jocular. The Conservative leader started with a joke about the prime minister's stamina after a marathon Commons' session on Tuesday when he took questions for more than three hours; there was laughter from MPs and a cautious smile from Burnham.

But if there was an early twinkle in the eye of either party leader their exchanges soon slipped into more familiar territory, trading barbs over tax and borrowing with Badenoch making claims of profligate government spending.

Burnham, despite his promises to end what he's called political "point scoring" was soon pointing the finger at the Tories for their economic record, referencing the budget of former Prime Minister Liz Truss while promising he'd deliver fiscal discipline.

He's not the first prime minister to pledge a new style of politics only to find it hard to dodge the adversarial nature of PMQs.

David Cameron said he'd end "Punch and Judy politics" when he became Tory leader only to find himself in regular political knockabouts across the despatch box.

But while the political barbs continued it's clear that Burnham is a more comfortable communicator than his predecessor. His real challenge will be delivering more than a change in tone.

The backdrop to his first few days as prime minister with Westminster in full swing has been the increased cost of borrowing – a global trend but one to which the UK is exposed and which looks likely to limit the chancellor's room for manoeuvre at the budget come the end of October.

Burnham has promised a transformational government but he's facing many of the same challenges as Sir Keir Starmer, with difficult decisions on defence spending, welfare and social care - to name just a few - hurtling towards him.

These are the pressure points his political opponents will seek to exploit, as evidenced by Badenoch's approach at Prime Minister's Questions when she quizzed him over plans for taxes, spending and borrowing.

Burnham pointed to his early actions in office, cutting VAT on domestic electricity bills and business rates for pubs and music venues as a sign of his priorities, but he gave little more away – leaning back on another familiar refrain that prime ministers don't write budgets from the despatch box.

In reality, it would be unfair to expect much more in the way of detail about Burnham's plans for the economy during his very first session of PMQs, but these are questions his government will eventually have to answer.

And what is clear is that despite the promise of a more consensual style of politics, when it comes to the substance there are sharp ideological differences across the Commons.

Burnham's diagnosis for the country's problems centres on privatisation and deindustrialisation over recent decades, as well as Brexit.

Badenoch disagrees, pointing instead to high taxes and spending as constraints on economic growth.

While Burnham's early weeks in office have seen a shift in style with a summer tour around the country and heavy social media presence, the economic arguments between him and his political opponents remain, and now Westminster is back in session there will likely be a clamour for more detail about his planned direction.

Today's Prime Minister's Questions is a taste of what's to come.

As well as smart communications, the choices the prime minister makes against a tricky economic background will take careful navigation if he's to deliver the optimistic future he's promised.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra on Wednesday slammed the party's rebel MPs for seeking additional time to respond to notices issued to them by the Lok Sabha secretariat.While talking to reporters, Mahua said that the rebel MPs' inability to respond within the stipulated period shows that they know they are in the wrong."We have filed 20 disqualification petitions against MPs who were elected on TMC tickets but joined hands with the BJP. articles.summary: NOIDA: Police have busted an inter-district gang allegedly involved in stealing from locked flats in housing societies and arrested three people, incl.
articles.body: NOIDA: Police have busted an inter-district gang allegedly involved in stealing from locked flats in housing societies and arrested three people, including a woman.The accused were arrested near a cremation ground in Sector 123.During interrogation, the suspects allegedly confessed to more than 100 thefts in Noida and several other districts of Uttar Pradesh.The arrested accused have been identified as 30-year-old Kailash alias Diwakar of Bulandshahr, 32-year-old Irfan alias Imran of Ghaziabad, and 24-year-old Sonali of Saharsa, Bihar.According to police, all three were currently living in different parts of Noida.Police recovered gold and silver jewellery, five laptops, two tablets, six mobile phones and Rs 3.50 lakh in cash from the accused.An Ertiga car allegedly used in the crimes and a vehicle registration plate suspected to be fabricated were also seized.Additional DCP Manisha Singh said the gang members would first enter housing societies wearing caps and masks and conduct reconnaissance of flats.They allegedly identified homes that appeared to be locked and assessed the possibility of finding cash, jewellery and electronic items inside.After identifying a target, the suspects would leave the society and return later in the Ertiga.Police said the accused deliberately covered their faces to prevent their identities from being clearly captured by CCTV cameras. They allegedly targeted jewellery, cash, mobile phones, laptops and other valuables.According to police, the gang would subsequently move the stolen property to different locations to dispose of it.Investigators are now verifying the suspects' alleged involvement in theft cases that have not yet been linked to the gang.From running cafes to allegedly targeting locked flatThe police probe uncovered a personal and criminal partnership between Diwakar and Sonali, who are in a relationship and live together.Police alleged that Sonali was closely involved in the gang’s operations, including identifying targets and carrying out reconnaissance, while Diwakar and his associate Irfan executed the thefts.Before turning to crime, Diwakar and Sonali had been running cafes.They first operated a cafe in Ghaziabad and later shifted their business to Noida.Police said mounting losses in the venture pushed the couple into financial distress, following which they began committing thefts.Cases registered in Noida and MathuraACP Sanchit Sharma said several cases are registered against the accused in Noida and Mathura.Kailash allegedly has a 2023 case registered at Phase 2 police station, besides theft cases at Sector 49, Sector 113 and Govind Nagar police station in Mathura.Irfan is also allegedly named in cases registered at Sector 49 and Sector 113 police stations in Noida and Govind Nagar in Mathura.Sonali has also been named in theft cases registered at Sector 49, Sector 113 and Govind Nagar.Police said some of the five recovered laptops have been linked to theft cases registered at Sector 113 and Sector 49. The two tablets were allegedly connected to a theft case registered at Sector 49.Network spread across districtsPolice suspect the gang's network extended beyond Noida.Investigators are trying to identify other members and determine where the stolen goods were sold. Two police teams have been formed to trace and arrest the remaining suspects.During interrogation, the accused allegedly revealed that stolen mobile phones and laptops were sold in different markets in Delhi.Police are now identifying traders and shopkeepers who may have purchased the stolen property.Officials said those found involved in knowingly dealing in stolen goods would also face arrest.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Noida | Silver Rate in Noida | Bank Holidays in Noida | Public Holidays in Noida | Noida AQI | Weather in Noida | Petrol Price in Noida | Diesel Price in Noida | CNG Price in Noida | LPG Price in NoidaStay updated with the latest Noida news. articles.title: 'Silicon Valley bodyshops specialize in faking up resumes': Trump aide Harmeet Dhillon on H-1B, PERM abuses
articles.summary: US News: President Donald Trump's aide and the Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights at the US Department of Justice, Harmeet Dhillon, spoke about her de.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's aide and the Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights at the US Department of Justice, Harmeet Dhillon, spoke about her department's action against the discrimination of Americans in US jobs. Speaking to Texas journalist Sara Gonzales, who busts alleged H-1B abuses on her show, Dhillon said she used to call the IT bodyshops 'software pimps' when she was working in Silicon Valley. Dhillon explained the economy of IT bodyshops or staffing companies that bring H-1Bs from overseas and then place them with clients. These staffing companies, she said, often trade these H-1Bs within themselves because they can't sponsor all of them, and she called it a 'human trafficking' operation.Dhillion said there are three to four middlemen who are getting their cuts from what a company is paying an engineer and hence the H-1B workers are getting way less salary and sometimes no salary. The last middleman is probably paying nothing to the engineer but the engineer can't protest because if they lose their jobs, they lose their visa and would be deported."Silicon Valley body shops specialize in faking up resumes. Some people might be extraordinary but a lot of this is fakery. And on top of that, these people are subject to restrictions on moving jobs, have lower salaries, don't have economic mobility, and can be exploited. It is a toxic situation, plus the job market excludes Americans," Dhillon said.On companies posting 'H-1B only' jobs, Dhillon said there are different types of visa categories and there's a lot of misconceptions around them."There's a category called PERM which requires an employers to first prove that they weren't able to find an American before they hire a foreign worker, And that's where we are finding quite a bit of fruad becauyse they're advertising these jobs in places that make it impossible for the normal American worker who applies for jobs online to even find out about it. So they'll apply in some obscure foriegn-only job board or in the middle of the night or something weird," Dhillon said, citing a recent case settlement with OpenAI.The H-1B visa program does not require employers to prove that an American was not available for the job. "However, our overarching federal civil rights laws make nationality discrimination a violation of federal employment law. Before this administration, no one considered anti-American discrimination to be national origin discrimination. But American is a national origin, whethet you are born here or a naturalized citizen. If we are being undercut, that's also discrimination," Dhillon said.PERM is the first step of Green Card sponsorship, where an employer submits an application to the Department of Labor for an employee's permanent residency. The employer has to certify that hiring a foreign worker won't displace American workers or lower their wages.OpenAI's PERM abuse settlementIn August, the Department of Justice secured a combined $3,200,000 settlement with OpenAI addressing allegations that the company discriminated against US workers and instead preferred workers with temporary employment visas.OpenAI did not advertise positions it sought to fill through the PERM program on its external job website. OpenAI also required applicants to mail paper applications for positions advertised as part of PERM recruitment, even though the company permitted electronic applications for other positions. In addition, OpenAI took other steps to discourage US workers from applying, such as advertising positions on the radio late at night.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: World war 2: The deadliest conflict in human history ended 81 years ago today
articles.summary: International News: The Second World War, widely regarded as the deadliest conflict in human history, ended 81 years ago on September 2, 1945. An estimated 70 million to .
articles.body: The Second World War, widely regarded as the deadliest conflict in human history, ended 81 years ago on September 2, 1945. An estimated 70 million to 85 million people, including civilians and military personnel, died in the war. More than 30 countries were involved in the conflict, which was fought across Europe, Asia, Africa and the Pacific.Germany, Italy and Japan formed the Axis powers, while Britain, the Soviet Union, the United States, China and France were among the major Allied powers.The war in Europe began on September 1, 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded Poland. Britain and France declared war on Germany two days later. Adolf Hitler's regime pursued territorial expansion and sought German dominance across Europe.Germany went on to occupy large parts of western Europe before invading the Soviet Union in June 1941. Japan was also expanding across Asia and had been fighting China since 1937. Japan's attack on the US naval base at Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, brought the United States into the war and expanded the conflict into a global war.The Axis powers initially made major territorial gains, but the Allies gradually turned the war in their favour. The Soviet victory at Stalingrad became a major turning point on the eastern front, while Allied forces advanced through North Africa and Italy.On June 6, 1944, Allied forces landed in Normandy, opening a major western European front against Germany. Soviet forces advanced from the east as Allied troops moved from the west. Hitler died by suicide on April 30, 1945, and Germany surrendered unconditionally on May 8, ending the war in Europe.The fighting continued against Japan in the Pacific. The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on August 6 and Nagasaki on August 9, while the Soviet Union declared war on Japan. Japan agreed to surrender, and on September 2, Japanese representatives formally signed the Instrument of Surrender aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay.The war left tens of millions dead and displaced, while large parts of Europe and Asia were devastated. Nazi Germany's persecuted millions of Jews and other groups in Europe.The conflict also reshaped global politics. The United States and Soviet Union emerged as the world's two dominant powers, beginning a decades-long Cold War. The United Nations was established in 1945 with the aim of maintaining international peace and preventing another global conflict.

articles.title: Six months of Trump's Iran war: America won battles, but where is the victory?
articles.summary: US News: When America's commander-in-chief President Donald Trump announced US strikes on Iran under the ambitious Operation Epic Fury in the early hours of Fe.
articles.body: When America's commander-in-chief President Donald Trump announced US strikes on Iran under the ambitious Operation Epic Fury in the early hours of February 28, there was little ambiguity about what Washington wanted from the campaign.This was not supposed to become another open-ended Middle Eastern war. The objective was to unleash overwhelming American military power, destroy Iran’s most dangerous capabilities, force Tehran to accept Washington’s terms and leave behind an Iran weakened enough that it could no longer pose the same strategic threat.Trump also appeared confident that the campaign would be relatively short. After his intervention in Venezuela earlier in 2026, he suggested that the war could last four or five weeks. Within days, he was already claiming that the military campaign was running ahead of schedule.“We're already substantially ahead of our time projections,” Trump said on March 2, just days after the campaign began, while adding that whatever time the operation ultimately required would be acceptable.Six months later, those words carry a very different weight.The war has stretched far beyond Trump's original timeline. Iran's nuclear infrastructure has suffered extensive damage, its conventional military has taken a severe beating and its leadership has been transformed. Yet Tehran has not surrendered.Even the killing of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran's longest-serving Supreme Leader and one of the most important figures in the history of the Islamic Republic, failed to bring down the government. Iran still retains missile capabilities, the Strait of Hormuz remains a major source of tension and Washington continues to negotiate over several of the same issues that were supposed to have been settled through military force.That leaves the central question as the war reaches its six-month mark: Trump may have won many of the battles, but did he achieve the objectives that took America into the war?The mission, in Trump's own wordsThe clearest way to understand what Trump wanted from the war is to return to what he said at the beginning of the campaign.On March 2, Trump laid out four objectives in unusually direct language. He said the US wanted to destroy Iran's missile capabilities and its capacity to produce new missiles, annihilate its navy, prevent Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon and stop the Iranian regime from arming, funding and directing militant groups beyond its borders.That was the core military mission.But Trump's rhetoric soon moved beyond missiles, ships and nuclear facilities. The war increasingly became a question about Iran's political system itself, with Trump at various points calling on Iranians to take control of their future, raising the possibility of regime change and demanding what he described as “UNCONDITIONAL SURRENDER.”Destroying missile launchers is one objective. Forcing Iran to abandon its strategic ambitions, surrender on American terms and potentially change the government in Tehran represents a far more ambitious undertaking.Six months into the war, those two ambitions have produced very different results.Iran's missiles: Devastated, but not erasedFew parts of Iran's military infrastructure escaped the opening waves of American and Israeli attacks. Missile launchers, production facilities, command centres and air-defence systems were repeatedly targeted as Washington and Jerusalem sought to dismantle Tehran's ability to wage war.By late March, Trump was already declaring major success. He said Iran's missiles had been “mostly decimated” while claiming that around 90% of its missiles and launchers had been knocked out.Trump subsequently went even further, declaring that Iran had effectively lost its conventional military.“I think the war is very complete, pretty much,” he said on March 9, claiming that Iran had no navy, communications system or air force.The battlefield, however, soon complicated that assessment.Iran continued firing missiles, the fighting continued and Tehran retained enough military capability to impose costs on American forces and regional allies.Iran's missile production and launch capabilities were severely degraded but did Washington achieve Trump's original promise of destroying Iran's ability to produce “brand new” missiles?Six months later, the answer appears to be no.Iran retains missile capabilities and, given sufficient time and resources, can rebuild parts of its arsenal. The result is therefore neither a clean American victory nor a straightforward failure.The nuclear question is even harderIf missiles represented the most visible military target, Iran's nuclear programme remained the strategic issue to which Trump repeatedly returned.The message from Washington was straightforward: Iran could not be allowed to acquire a nuclear weapon.Trump has overseen two major American military campaigns targeting Iran's nuclear ambitions, Operation Midnight Hammer in 2025 and Operation Epic Fury in 2026. This year's strikes inflicted enormous damage on Iran's nuclear infrastructure, and Trump subsequently described the programme as devastated.But there is a problem that airstrikes cannot easily solve: knowing exactly what remains.Six months into the war, Washington still lacks the certainty required to declare Iran's nuclear question permanently settled. International inspectors have faced enormous difficulties assessing the aftermath, while one of the most serious unresolved questions concerns Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium.Reuters reported in August that the IAEA had been unable to verify the location of roughly 440 kg of uranium enriched to 60%, leaving uncertainty about where the material was located and what Tehran might ultimately do with it.That goes to the heart of the nuclear problem.Destroying a facility does not necessarily mean destroying the underlying capability. Trump can point to craters, damaged buildings and destroyed infrastructure, while Iran can point to assets that are far harder to eliminate through airstrikes, including scientific knowledge, personnel and nuclear material.Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi has also maintained that the country's nuclear rights cannot simply be erased through military pressure.The nuclear objective remains one of the most important unresolved parts of Trump's war.Iran's military: The clearest American successIf there is one part of the war where the scoreboard is relatively straightforward, it is Iran's conventional military.The US and Israel have inflicted enormous damage on Iranian air defences, missile infrastructure, naval assets and command structures. The scale of that destruction would have been difficult to imagine before the war began, while the killing of senior commanders and destruction of military facilities further reduced Tehran's ability to wage a conventional conflict against the US.But military success and political success are not the same thing.Iran did not necessarily need to defeat the US in a conventional battle. Its more immediate requirement was to survive the campaign, preserve the state and retain enough military capability to prevent Washington from dictating the terms of the conflict entirely.And it has survived.The Iranian government remained in place even after Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed. The country's institutions continued functioning, while Tehran retained enough military capability to threaten American interests and keep the confrontation alive.That makes Trump's military achievement significant, but it also leaves the strategy for ending the war incomplete.Khamenei is gone, but the regime survivedThe death of Khamenei was arguably the most consequential single event of the war. For decades, he had been the central figure of the Islamic Republic, and his removal created the possibility that Iran's political system could collapse under the shock.That did not happen.Iran's political system absorbed the blow and produced a new leadership structure, demonstrating that the Islamic Republic was considerably more resilient than a campaign focused on eliminating senior leaders may have assumed.Washington never maintained a perfectly consistent public formulation over whether regime change was an official war objective. Trump nevertheless repeatedly encouraged Iranians to challenge their rulers and spoke about the possibility of a political transformation.The war did change Iran's leadership, but it did not change Iran's regime.The proxy network: Weakened, not wiped outAnother important element of Trump's original mission was to prevent Iran from arming, funding and directing militant groups across the Middle East.Here too, the war has inflicted substantial damage.Iran's ability to provide weapons, money and logistical support has been weakened by the destruction of military infrastructure and the collapse in oil revenues. Yet the regional network has not simply disappeared.Many groups linked to Tehran possess their own organisational structures, local political interests and independent sources of support. That means even a severely weakened Iran can retain influence across the region.The war may have altered the regional balance considerably, but it has not erased the network.Then came the demand: 'Unconditional Surrender'Perhaps no Trump phrase better captures the evolution of the conflict than “UNCONDITIONAL SURRENDER”.The demand left little room for compromise, and Iran unsurprisingly rejected it. Iranian officials repeatedly insisted that Tehran would negotiate only on terms that protected its sovereignty and security.In May, Iranian parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf told Pakistan's army chief and field marshal Asim Munir that Tehran would not compromise in negotiations with Washington. By August, foreign minister Araghchi was even more explicit, saying that Iran had not yet decided to restart negotiations with the US.Araghchi later said talks would not resume while Washington was violating the interim agreement reached in June.The positions of the two sides had effectively become mirror images of one another.Washington wanted Iran to make major concessions before US pressure was eased, while Tehran wanted the pressure reduced before making significant concessions.That deadlock has helped keep the war alive.From bombs to sanctionsBy summer, another shift was becoming increasingly visible as the war proved difficult to sustain through military force alone.The US had spent enormous sums and consumed large quantities of precision munitions, prompting Washington to lean harder on economic pressure and sanctions. Trump's administration sought to squeeze Iranian oil revenues, punish countries and companies dealing with Tehran and isolate the Iranian economy.In August, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that Washington was preparing what he described as the “toughest sanctions in history” against Iran.The calculation is straightforward: Iran may eventually accept terms it has rejected on the battlefield if its economy becomes too weak to sustain the confrontation.But Iran is already paying a huge price.President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iranian foreign trade had fallen by nearly 35% because of sanctions and the naval blockade, while Reuters reported that inflation had reached 66%.Yet Tehran has not capitulated.Pezeshkian has acknowledged the economic pain while continuing to insist that Iran will not surrender its core interests.Strait of HormuzPerhaps the most striking change in Trump's war objectives has been the growing importance of the Strait of Hormuz.At the beginning of the conflict, the central strategic question was Iran's nuclear programme. Six months later, one of Washington's most urgent concerns is whether ships can safely pass through one of the world's most important energy chokepoints.Trump has repeatedly claimed that Hormuz remains open and functioning, but the reality has been considerably more complicated. Iran has used its position around the waterway as leverage in negotiations, turning the strait into one of the most important bargaining chips in the conflict.In August, Tehran said a deal with Oman over control of the Strait was close, while warning that such an agreement would not automatically reopen the waterway.Trump, meanwhile, increasingly made the reopening of Hormuz part of his demands. On August 2, he said the US had held off a “massive attack” on Iran to facilitate a deal that would end Tehran's nuclear ambitions and reopen the Strait.The shift is revealing.A war that began with the stated objective of destroying Iran's military capabilities had become, at least in part, a negotiation over access to a waterway that Tehran can threaten and use as leverage even if it cannot control the strait indefinitely.So, where does Trump stand now?The answer depends largely on which version of Trump's mission is being measured.If the objective was to destroy Iran's conventional military, Washington has come close to achieving it. If the aim was to cripple Iran's missile programme, the United States has inflicted extraordinary damage but has not eliminated the capability.If the objective was to destroy Iran's nuclear infrastructure, much of the physical infrastructure has been devastated, but the ultimate nuclear question remains unresolved.If Washington wanted to break Iran's regional network, that network has been significantly weakened but continues to survive.If the objective was to bring down the Iranian regime, that has not happened.If Trump wanted Tehran to accept unconditional surrender, that has plainly not happened.And if the goal was to end the war quickly, Trump's original timeline has been decisively missed.Perhaps the clearest measure of that gap can be found in Trump's own language.In March, he described the war as “very complete, pretty much”. By the end of March, he said the “core objectives” were nearing completion and suggested the conflict could end within two or three weeks.By July, his message had changed again, with Trump saying the United States would either make a deal with Iran or “finish the job”.By August, he was saying Washington had held off another major attack in the hope of reaching a deal.At the six-month mark, the fighting remained capable of flaring back up.The evolution of Trump's language tells its own story.Iran's answer: We are still hereTehran's response has remained remarkably consistent despite the scale of the devastation.Iranian officials acknowledge the enormous damage inflicted on the country and the economic pressure created by the war and sanctions. They nevertheless reject the idea that Iran has been defeated.Pezeshkian said on September 1 that Iran would immediately reciprocate if Washington returned to its commitments under the June memorandum. He also reiterated Tehran's willingness to guarantee freedom of navigation through Hormuz if the United States adhered to the agreement.It was an unusually revealing statement because, after six months of war, Iran was still offering a negotiated route out of the conflict.But it was not offering surrender.The real test is no longer what America can destroyIran has been badly wounded. Its economy is under extraordinary pressure, its military has been devastated and its leadership has been transformed.But the state survives.And Iran retains the ability to complicate the world's energy system through the Strait of Hormuz.That leaves Trump in an uncomfortable middle ground.He can legitimately claim major military victories, but he still needs the political victory that can convert those battlefield gains into a lasting settlement.That is why, six months after Trump said the US was “substantially ahead” of its timetable, the most important battlefield of the Iran war may no longer be Iran's skies or its missile bases. It may be the negotiating table.The ultimate measure of Trump's Iran war will not be the number of targets destroyed, the number of missiles eliminated or the amount of military infrastructure reduced to rubble.It will be whether Tehran ultimately accepts a settlement that Washington can present as a victory, and whether that settlement lasts longer than the last ceasefire.For now, neither question has been answered.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Happy Krishna Janmashtami 2026: Wishes, messages, quotes, images, Facebook & WhatsApp status
articles.summary: Krishna Janmashtami 2026 will be observed on Friday, September 4, and this year the celebration carries a bit of poetic weight, marking the 5,253rd bi.
articles.body: Krishna Janmashtami 2026 will be observed on Friday, September 4, and this year the celebration carries a bit of poetic weight, marking the 5,253rd birth anniversary of Lord Krishna according to reports. The festival commemorates his birth at midnight in Mathura, and devotees across the country will observe the same rituals that have marked this night for generations: a day-long fast broken only after the midnight Nishita Kaal puja, temples decorated and packed for Janmotsav celebrations, and children dressed up as young Krishna and Radha for the occasion. Mathura and Vrindavan remain the beating heart of the festival, drawing millions for the midnight celebrations, but homes and temples everywhere mark the night in their own way, through bhajans, Raas Leela performances, and the joyfully chaotic Dahi Handi tradition. As families and friends prepare to celebrate, here's a complete collection of wishes, quotes, and ideas to help you mark Krishna Janmashtami 2026 properly, wherever you are.Heartfelt WhatsApp wishes and messagesFor a message that goes beyond a quick forward, these carry a warmer, more personal tone, well suited for close family or anyone you want to reach with something genuine on this sacred night."May Lord Krishna's flute fill your life with the same joy and melody it brought to Vrindavan. Happy Janmashtami!""On this blessed night, may Bal Gopal bless your home with happiness, peace, and prosperity. Happy Krishna Janmashtami!""May you find the same wisdom Krishna gave Arjuna, the courage to face life with clarity and calm. Happy Janmashtami!""Wishing you a Janmashtami filled with devotion, sweetness, and the mischief of little Krishna himself.""May the divine light of Krishna's birth guide you through every challenge this year. Happy Janmashtami to you and your family.""Sending you love and blessings this Janmashtami, may your home always echo with 'Hare Krishna'.""Just like Yashoda's love for baby Krishna, may your life be filled with unconditional love and joy. Happy Janmashtami!""May Lord Krishna's blessings remove every obstacle from your path this year. Janmashtami ki hardik shubhkamnayein!""This Janmashtami, may your heart find the same devotion Radha held for Krishna. Wishing you peace and happiness.""Here's to celebrating the birth of the one who taught us that even in darkness, light always finds a way. Happy Janmashtami!"Quotes and teachings to add to your messageA short line drawn from Krishna's teachings in the Bhagavad Gita, or simply about his life, adds real depth to a Janmashtami wish. These work well tucked into a longer message or shared as a standalone thought for the day."Do your duty without attachment to the results; that's the essence of what Krishna taught Arjuna on the battlefield.""Krishna reminds us that whenever there's a decline in righteousness, a greater force rises to restore balance.""The soul is eternal, Krishna taught, it is never born and never dies, it simply changes form.""Peace comes not from controlling the world around you, but from mastering the one within, a lesson straight from the Gita.""Krishna's life reminds us that even divinity finds joy in simplicity, a flute, a few friends, and the open fields of Vrindavan.""Change is the only constant, Krishna taught, and wisdom lies in accepting it rather than resisting it.""Devotion offered with a pure heart matters more to Krishna than any grand gesture.""Even a leaf or a flower, offered with love, is enough, Krishna's own words on true devotion."Instagram captions and Facebook status ideasFor anyone posting a Bal Gopal idol, a Dahi Handi celebration, or a beautifully decorated jhula today, these captions and status lines are built to match the mood."Radhe Radhe! Celebrating the birth of the one who taught the world to love without conditions. #Janmashtami2026""Little feet, big blessings. Happy Janmashtami to all!""Devotion in every diya, joy in every bhajan. Happy Krishna Janmashtami!""Nand ke Anand Bhayo, Jai Kanhaiya Lal Ki! Happy Janmashtami""May the mischief of Kanha bring some lightness into your life today.""Fasting, praying, and waiting for midnight, Janmashtami spirit in full swing.""Hare Krishna, Hare Rama, sending love and light this Janmashtami.""Decorated the jhula, lit the diyas, ready for midnight. Happy Janmashtami, everyone!""Some celebrations are worth staying up till midnight for. Jai Shri Krishna ""From Vrindavan to your living room, may Krishna's blessings reach every home. Happy Janmashtami!"Picture and image ideas worth capturing todayCertain shots come up again and again on Janmashtami for good reason, they capture the day's spirit perfectly. A close-up of a beautifully decorated Bal Gopal idol, often dressed in tiny new clothes with a peacock feather crown, remains one of the most shared images every year. Photos of the jhula or cradle, decorated with flowers and fairy lights for the midnight celebration, work beautifully as a festive post. If there's a Dahi Handi event nearby, action shots of the human pyramid mid-formation capture genuine energy and excitement. And for something more reflective, a simple photo of a lit diya beside a small Krishna idol, taken right around midnight, tends to be the one people remember longest.A quick note on timing for tonight's celebrationsFor anyone planning their own midnight puja, the sacred Ashtami Tithi this year begins in the early hours of September 4 and continues until just after midnight into September 5, with the Rohini Nakshatra active for a significant stretch of the day as well. The actual moment of celebration, the Nishita Kaal, falls right around midnight, the exact window devotees traditionally regard as the true moment of Krishna's birth in Mathura. Most families plan their fast-breaking and final aarti around this precise window, so it's worth checking local panchang timings for your city if you're observing the fast strictly.Whether it's a heartfelt WhatsApp message sent before the fast begins, a quote from the Gita shared with quiet reflection, or a midnight photo of the jhula lit up in diyas, Krishna Janmashtami 2026 gives everyone, near Mathura or far from it, a reason to pause and celebrate a night that's been marked with devotion for over five thousand years. Happy Janmashtami to you and everyone you choose to share it with tonight.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: Drumcree: 'Orange Order put us through hell' say Garvaghy Road residents
articles.summary: Breandán Mac Cionnaith said the Orange Order should be apologising to the people rather than marching in the area.
articles.body:
A residents group in Portadown has accused the Orange Order of putting their community "through hell" with parades.

Breandán Mac Cionnaith, a spokesperson for Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition, said the order should be apologising to the people rather than marching in the area.

Details of their planned parade are expected to be announced at a news conference in the town on Thursday morning.

In an interview with BBC News NI, Mac Cionnaith said that if any talks were to take place with the Orange Order, residents of Garvaghy Road should set the agenda.

"It should be up to the host community to set the agenda, not the visitors," he said.

"The community here has been put through hell by the Orange Order - 1995, 96, 97, 98, continue on.

"All those years the Orange Order have created hassle for this community. Never once was there an apology, never once did they ever say sorry, never once did they ever say 'we've had our march, there's another route, we'll take it home'."

The Orange Order have always said they had peaceful intent and the root cause of any violence in the 1990s was the fact that they were prevented from walking the traditional route of their parade. They accused the residents group of being intransigent.

He rejected suggestions by some unionists that he does represent the overall view of residents in the area.

He said: "I think if anybody goes out onto the Garvaghy Road now and takes a walk round and just asks people… they'll get the same response - 'no, it's over, put it to bed once and for all'."

He said: "The Orange Order has never, ever accepted the right of this community, or those who represent it, to put forward another possibility, that there should be no Orange march."

No date has been set for the order's planned parade but Sunday 27 September has been mentioned as a possibility.

The Parades Commission will access any notification of a parade and decide what restrictions, if any, to put on it.

The Orange Order and unionist politicians say an Orange Order parade down the Garvaghy Road should be allowed.

DUP leader Gavin Robinson said: "There is no benefit to good, positive cross-community relations if that means that one section of the community can deny their neighbours from walking home from church, none whatsoever."

It is expected that the planned parade would involve a walk to a service at Drumcree Church of Ireland from Portadown town centre that does not include the Garvaghy Road but would include it on the homeward leg of the march.

articles.title: In 1989, teacher Gary Greff returned to his shrinking North Dakota hometown and learned to weld; his plan to lure travelers became a 32-mile highway of giant sculptures, including a Guinness world record
articles.summary: US News: On a stretch of North Dakota highway where golden fields meet an endless prairie sky, a giant metal knight stands guard over a castle, protecting it f.
articles.body: On a stretch of North Dakota highway where golden fields meet an endless prairie sky, a giant metal knight stands guard over a castle, protecting it from a fire-breathing dragon. It sounds like something out of a fairy tale, but in Regent these giant figures are part of a very real roadside attraction that grew from one man’s desire to put a fading hometown on the map. For more than 30 years, former teacher and school principal Gary Greff has been using scrap metal to create gigantic works of art along the Enchanted Highway, one of the more unusual attractions in southwestern North Dakota. After a career in education, Greff returned to his hometown of Regent in 1989. He didn’t go down the expected path. Instead, he focused on a crazy idea: Using giant sculptures to draw travelers off Interstate 94 and into his struggling community. He'd never welded before. He learned the skill from local farmers, and his first major work, the Tin Family, was installed two years later in 1991. The concept was simple, but ambitious: travelers could be persuaded to make a detour for something truly exceptional, while they might just drive past a typical small town. The experiment finally blossomed into the Enchanted Highway, a 32-mile stretch from Exit 72 on I-94 to Regent with giant scrap-metal sculptures along the way.Huge sculptures in the prairiesThere are now eight sculpture scenes along the highway, including giant grasshoppers, a massive fisherman-themed creation and the Tin Family. One of the most notable is Geese in Flight, completed in August 2001 by Greff. It stands 110 feet high, 154 feet wide, and weighs 157,659 pounds. It earned a Guinness World Record for the world’s largest scrap-metal sculpture in 2002. Greff's latest project of 2024 took the fantasy theme to another level.A knight, a dragon and a breathing spectacleSir Albert is a giant armored knight, 41 feet tall, built to guard the Enchanted Castle in Regent. His opponent is a 42-foot-tall green dragon, 100 feet from nose to tail. The sculptures were completed after nine years of work. This pair is meant to interact with visitors, as opposed to the earlier static creations along the highway. The dragon breathes fire, makes smoke and lets out a battle cry. The knight shall answer in the setting of an animated story about a peasant, a magic potion and a heroic battle.Creating a future for the highwayNow 75, Greff has no plans to stop creating. Concrete mixer tanks are being converted into gigantic spider bodies, and already a 70-foot spiderweb is being spun behind the Enchanted Castle, states an online report. Meanwhile, the Friends of the Enchanted Highway Foundation have been working to make sure the sculptures live on after Greff’s lifetime. Maintaining the existing attractions costs about $70,000 a year, the foundation is seeking grants, corporate sponsorships, donations and an endowment to establish a sustainable source of funding. The group hopes to recruit welders, volunteers and develop ideas for an interpretive center that traces Greff’s story.From a struggling town to a rest stopOver the years the highway has become a major thoroughfare, bringing visitors that might otherwise have driven through the region without stopping. Nestled among wheat fields and sunflower fields, the Enchanted Highway has become more than just a series of giant sculptures. It’s the culmination of Greff’s decades-long bid to turn imagination into economic opportunity, and to ensure a small town in North Dakota remains anything but forgotten.Images Courtesy: North Dakota Living and Enchanted HighwayCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Reprehensible act of vandalism’: India condemns demolition of century-old Hindu temple in Pakistan, seeks probe
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday expressed deep concern over reports of the destruction of a historic Hindu temple in Pakistan's Punjab province and call.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday expressed deep concern over reports of the destruction of a historic Hindu temple in Pakistan's Punjab province and called on the Pakistani government to conduct a prompt and transparent investigation into the incident.Responding to media queries, ministry of external affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India “unequivocally” condemned the reported vandalism of the century-old place of worship in Siraj village in Narowal.“We have noted with deep concern the disturbing reports of the destruction of a historic Hindu temple in village Siraj, Narowal, Pakistan. We unequivocally condemn this reprehensible act of vandalism against a century old minority place of worship,” Jaiswal said.India flags authorities' 'apathy'The MEA said the apparent failure of authorities to protect the temple was alarming and raised concerns over the safety and religious freedoms of minority communities in Pakistan.“The apparent apathy of authorities and failure to protect this century-old temple is alarming. Such incidents are a stark reminder of the continuing vulnerability of minority communities and the egregious violations of their religious freedoms and places of worship in Pakistan,” Jaiswal said.India called upon Pakistan to investigate the incident and ensure that those responsible are held accountable.“We call upon the Government of Pakistan to conduct a prompt and transparent investigation into this incident and ensure that those responsible are held fully accountable,” the MEA spokesperson said.India also urged Pakistan to take immediate steps to restore the temple and ensure the safety and security of minority communities and their cultural heritage.“Furthermore, the Government of Pakistan must take immediate remedial measures to restore the desecrated temple and fulfill its primary obligation to guarantee the safety, security and well-being of all its minority citizens and their cultural heritage,” Jaiswal added.Temple's destruction triggered calls for restorationThe more than 100-year-old temple in Siraj village, around 130 km from Lahore, was demolished on August 21.Minority groups alleged that religious zealots had targeted the site to absorb its land into an adjacent madrassa, while Pakistan's Evacuee Trust Property Board (ETPB) maintained that the structure had collapsed following torrential rains.ETPB senior official Rana Iftikhar acknowledged the temple's historical significance, saying it was “more than 100 to 125 years old”, while maintaining that the land on which the temple stood had not been leased to anyone.The demolition prompted demands from minority groups and local Hindu community leaders for an investigation and the restoration of the temple.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Dad who won only a cabbage in 1977 meat draw scoops £4 million Georgian mansion in Bath with wife, £250,000 cash, mortgage-free home and £140,000 worth of furnishings through Omaze
articles.summary: UK News: A father who once won nothing more than a cabbage in a 1977 meat draw has now landed a dramatically bigger prize - a £4 million Georgian mansion in Ba.
articles.body: A father who once won nothing more than a cabbage in a 1977 meat draw has now landed a dramatically bigger prize - a £4 million Georgian mansion in Bath, Somerset, along with £250,000 in cash.According to SWNS, Wayne Wood, 64, from Loughborough, Leicestershire, and his wife Catherine, 53, won the historic property through an Omaze prize draw. The couple, who have been married for 18 years and have two teenage children, will also receive the property mortgage-free, with stamp duty and legal fees covered, as well as £140,000 worth of furnishings.From a cabbage to a £4 million mansionWayne said his previous prize was a cabbage, which he won nearly five decades ago after entering a meat draw with friends.“A £4 million mansion is quite the upgrade from a cabbage!” he said.“I remember I was with my brass band friends on a trip somewhere up north in the 70s and we all entered a meat draw, buying a load of tickets for 2p each, and I ended up winning the cabbage. It’s been a running joke ever since.”Despite the humble win, Wayne never stopped entering prize draws and said he had always dreamed of winning a house.“I’m a dreamer who always wanted to win a big house, that cabbage started my winning streak!” he added.Wayne, who works in marketing, had been an Omaze subscriber for four years, although Catherine was unaware of his subscription.‘I thought I was being punked’When Wayne received the news about the latest prize, he initially suspected it was a prank.“I thought I was being ‘punked’ at first, so I didn’t say anything to my wife until I was 100 per cent sure,” he said.The father said he had always dreamed of owning a large home with a great view, making the win difficult to comprehend.“We have a very lovely life with beautiful children, but you’ve got to keep dreaming and not just settle for less,” he said.Catherine admitted she initially paid little attention when Wayne told her he might have won.“He would win little things here or there, but I’ve never really paid any attention, so even when he first messaged to say he might have won a prize, I just ignored it,” she said.She added that while Wayne had always been the bigger dreamer in the family, she was now convinced that his optimism had paid off.Historic Bath home has a wine cellar and Coach HouseThe property was built in the early 1800s by celebrated Bath architect John Pinch and comes with a range of period features and luxury amenities.The Georgian villa includes a wine cellar, underfloor heating, landscaped gardens and a separate Coach House for guests.Wayne said the family had never previously visited Bath and was stunned by the city.“Just last week we were on holiday visiting a UNESCO World Heritage site in Greece, and now we own a house in a UNESCO site – I can’t believe it!” he said.“We’ve never been to Bath before and didn’t realise how beautiful this place is, and now we own one of the best houses here.”Catherine wants a Bridgerton-themed partyCatherine, a fan of Bridgerton, is already imagining celebrations at the new property.She said the house felt like something straight out of the Netflix period drama, which is partly filmed in Bath.“It’s like something out of Bridgerton – I felt like I was on the Bridgerton set!” she said.“Bridgerton is filmed in Bath and my sisters and I are big fans, so we’re already thinking about having a Bridgerton themed party here. How perfect would that be?”She also joked that the multiple fridges and wine cellar made the property ideal for entertaining.Wayne wishes his late mother could have seen the winThe life-changing win has also been an emotional one for Wayne, who lost his mother last month.He said he wished she had been alive to see the family’s extraordinary new home.“I used to call her my ‘one in a million’ and now I’ve won this home which is worth millions, she would have loved it,” he said.“I wish she knew about this, maybe she did, maybe she’s looking down on us, maybe she had something to do with this. If she was still here, she’d be ecstatic.”£250,000 cash could cover years of running costsIf the family chooses to keep the property, the additional £250,000 prize money could help cover its running costs for years.Alternatively, local estate agents estimate that the property could command a long-term rental value of between £9,000 and £10,000 a month if the couple decides to let it out.Matt Pohlson, founder and CEO of Omaze, said the organisation was delighted that Wayne and Catherine had won the Bath home while supporting English Heritage.He said Omaze had now raised more than £150 million for good causes across the UK.Alongside the guaranteed £1 million raised through the draw, Omaze has also committed a further £3.5 million through a separate multi-year grant to support future projects at Stonehenge. This takes its total contribution to English Heritage to £4.5 million.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'New peaks of lethality': IAF tests Khagantak-243; all about long range glide bomb
articles.summary: News News: The Indian Air Force has successfully conducted the drop trial of the indigenously designed and developed Khagantak-243, a long-range glide bomb, mark.
articles.body: The Indian Air Force has successfully conducted the drop trial of the indigenously designed and developed Khagantak-243, a long-range glide bomb, marking a significant milestone in India's development of indigenous stand-off strike weapons.In a post on X, the Indian Air Force said the trial of the Khagantak-243 successfully met all objectives, calling it a significant milestone for the IAF and Indian industry. The force said the test demonstrated new levels of lethality through Atmanirbhar Bharat, Make in India and defence innovation.The IAF had earlier placed an order with Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) for an unspecified number of Khagantak-243 munitions, with the contract value not disclosed. The weapon has been developed collaboratively by BEL and JSR Dynamics, with JSR Dynamics providing the bomb's body and control systems and BEL supplying its electronics and guidance subsystems.The Khagantak-243 is an indigenously designed and developed long-range glide bomb intended to provide the IAF with a stand-off precision strike capability. Unlike a conventional free-fall bomb, a glide bomb can travel towards its target after being released from an aircraft, allowing strikes from greater distances.Khagantak-243The Khagantak-243 is a 300-kg-class airborne long-range stand-off precision-guided glide bomb developed jointly by JSR Dynamics and Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL).The weapon is designed to be released from a fighter aircraft and then glide towards its target using its aerodynamic wings and control surfaces, allowing the aircraft to attack targets from a stand-off distance rather than flying directly over them. The Khagantak-243 has a cylindrical body, swivel-type mid-body glide wings and five aft control surfaces.The Khagantak-243 has a reported range of more than 140 km when released from an altitude of around 12,000 metres.The bomb is equipped with a Mk 81 general-purpose blast-fragmentation warhead containing 125 kg of explosive fill. The Khagantak family has a modular design, allowing different warhead and guidance configurations depending on the mission and customer requirements.The Su-30MKI was identified as the initial platform for flight testing of the Khagantak-243, with potential integration with other aircraft also reported.

articles.title: Trump suggests renaming Strait of Hormuz ‘Trump Strait’ amid escalating US-Iran conflict
articles.summary: Middle East News: US President Donald Trump has suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz as the “Trump Strait”, saying the move could be considered after what he describ.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz as the “Trump Strait”, saying the move could be considered after what he described as the United States gaining control of the strategic waterway.“Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.Trump has repeatedly claimed that the United States controls the Strait of Hormuz. The White House said on August 28 that US forces had established control of the waterway, citing the clearance of Iranian mines, the movement of nearly 1,500 commercial vessels under US protection and the redirection of vessels attempting to breach the US blockade.The latest remark comes as the confrontation between Washington and Tehran has intensified. US central command said American forces completed a wave of strikes against Iranian military targets on September 1, including air-defence sites, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications facilities.The United States has also maintained a naval blockade against Iranian ports. CENTCOM said in July that the blockade would target maritime traffic entering and leaving Iranian ports, while US forces would continue supporting vessels not violating the blockade.The Strait of Hormuz has emerged as a central flashpoint in the conflict because of its importance for commercial shipping and energy supplies.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
